subtopic: OUTER SPACE-INDICATION OF INTENTION TO RATIFY TREATY

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Hellyer (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: OUTER SPACE-INDICATION OF INTENTION TO RATIFY TREATY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to inform hon. members that it is the intention of Canada to ratify, as soon as possible, the treaty on principles governing activities of states in the exploration and use of outer space including the moon and other celestial bodies. Order in council authorization for such ratification is being sought, as the house standing committee on external affairs was informed last Thursday.
Perhaps I should first of all say a word or two about the reason why ratification by Canada of this treaty is a matter of some urgency. This is because the three depositary countries, the United Kingdom, the United States of America and the Soviet union are themselves in the process of ratifying the treaty in accordance with their respective constitutional procedures.
It is expected that, following the precedents which were established for the limited nuclear test ban agreement in 1963, the three governments will soon agree on the date upon which each will deposit its instrument of ratification with the other two, as prescribed in the treaty, thereby bringing it into force. Once this has happened other countries will be able to deposit their own instruments of ratification with any or all of the three depositary nations, and thus bring the treaty into effect for themselves.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
Canada, as a member of the 28 state United Nations outer space committee, played an active part in the negotiations which culminated in the adoption of the text of the treaty. Since Canada was one of the first countries to sign the treaty, on January 27, 1967, it would serve to emphasize the importance which we attach to it if Canada were also to be among the first countries to ratify it.
This treaty, three copies of which I am now tabling in English and in French, is intended to ensure that outer space, the moon and other celestial bodies will be explored and used only for peaceful purposes and that there can be no national appropriation of such bodies. Of particular significance in this respect are those provisions which state that parties to the treaty undertake not to place in orbit around the earth any body carrying nuclear weapons or any other weapons of mass destruction, instal such weapons in celestial bodies or station such weapons in outer space. The establishment of military bases, installations and fortifications, the testing of any type of weapons and the conduct of military manoeuvres on celestial bodies are also forbidden. These terms incorporate the main ideas expressed in the 1963 United Nations resolution on outer space and represent a significant step forward in the achievement of multilateral arms control arrangements.
The treaty emphasizes freedom of scientific investigation on celestial bodies and in outer space. It also stresses co-operation among states, both in avoiding the contamination of outer space and in the dissemination of information on conditions which might cause harm to the health or affect the safety of astronauts. In order further to promote such international co-operation, states party to the treaty are to consider, on the basis of equality, requests from other parties to build tracking facilities on their territory for observing the flight of space objects which the requesting nation has launched. The treaty stipulates that if the request is considered favourably all the necessary terms and conditions are to be arranged by negotiations. Should these terms and conditions prove unacceptable to the host nations, however,

In conclusion, I should also point out that the treaty does not, by its terms, requii-e any legislative action on the part of those countries which become parties to it. It is, rather, a significant forward step in the codification and formalization of principles of international law, many of which were earlier set out in the 1963 United Nations resolution on outer space. It is because of this country's active role in the space field and in the international legal sphere, and because of the importance of the treaty for the development of the rule of law in outer space, that it would be particularly appropriate for Canada, by ratification, to be among the first countries that formally accept the principles which the treaty enshrines.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: OUTER SPACE-INDICATION OF INTENTION TO RATIFY TREATY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a forward step internationally. I recall, back in January 1958 I believe it was, speaking to the Canadian Bar Association on the subject of the need for an international control agreement in respect of outer space. The intervening years have not seen much progress in this direction. However, this forward step is beclouded by the fact that within the last few days communist China has been able to explode a nuclear bomb. Communist China is not a member of this organization, being outside the pale internationally. This underlines the necessity of controlling outer space against its potential use for war purposes; this is emphasized by what has taken place. It also underlines the need to ensure that communist China shall be in a position in which it will be subject to the control which civilized men and women everywhere desire over this powerful deterrent, having both hope and fear for mankind in the possibility of improper use, or use for warlike purposes.
Mr. Speaker, this treaty for the control of Mr. Speaker, this treaty for the control of armaments in outer space is a great forward step for the human race. I am very glad Canada is to be one of the first nations to attach its signature to it. However, the fact still remains that the republic of mainland China is not only not a signatory of the nonproliferation treaty, but also not likely to be a signatory to this treaty.
Surely this ought to point out the need for Canada along with other peace loving countries to use all the influence it can to bring mainland China into the community of nations, and to attempt to seat her in the United


Nations so she can become a part of the world community and be persuaded of the necessity, first of signing the non-proliferation treaty and also the treaty in respect of the control of arms in outer space. I think the governments concerned are to be congratulated in that we have taken the first step toward reducing the possibility of a conflict in outer space, and I hope they will now apply themselves with equal diligence to get peace on earth.

subtopic: OUTER SPACE-INDICATION OF INTENTION TO RATIFY TREATY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the statement the hon. Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer) has just made on the ratification of an outer space treaty truly proves that men are spurred on by science. I trust the ratification of this treaty will be conducive to better results with regard to the control of nuclear arms on earth. I am proud and I think we should all be proud, of the part Canada wants to play in such control.
Although the minister smiled repeatedly during his statement, we have every reason to consider the matter as most serious, since a power on this earth-that is on the planet earth-has already started drainage works on the moon, even though it is said there is no moisture up there. The fact that the countries plan to solve space problems is a serious factor and Canada, in being one of the first to ratify the treaty, prove its interest in world affairs and its willingness to move ahead.

We are gratified, along with other members of the house, that this small measure of progress has been made and that Canada has been able to take her share in this regard.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF ENERGY, MINES AND RESOURCES
speechtext:
We have been watching with interest for some time the machinations of Canada's oil and gas policy as it affects Trans-Canada Pipe Lines in particular. We are certainly not very pleased with the decision which came out of Washington through the federal power commission approving without strings the application of Great Lakes Power to transmit our gas through the United States.
It is important to note in this case the development of events over which we in Canada have no control but which in the long run may have an effect contrary to Canadian interests. I have been following these developments carefully. I do not intend to beat the subject to death, since the decision has now been made, but I am surprised at the position this government has chosen to take up. The Canadian people expect their government to act in Canada's interests. They expect we should not be a bad neighbour to the United States but that along with that we should think first and foremost of ourselves. The original statement made by the Prime Minister when this matter was first discussed early in October, 1966, was a good one, but the decisions that have been taken since have vacillated from bad to good and back to bad again.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
I am particularly surprised that the minister has taken this course. One reason for my surprise is that he is a young, very capable and aggressive minister. He is a French Canadian, and in my opinion French Canadians have been more nationalistic than any other Canadians. As a matter of fact many of us did not really think about being Canadians until French Canadians raised the question of their brand of Canadianism being different from ours, thereby forcing us to examine what nationalism means in other parts of Canada.
Not many years ago the minister was going around saying that everybody in the province of Quebec should be a Quebec nationalist and that everybody employed by the national government should speak French. He advocated that we be nationalistic in a narrow sense. But all of a sudden the minister has adopted another position which eventually he will rue.
At the end of October, 1966, the minister went to the United States where he addressed the Independent Petroleum Association of America. I would like to quote from his address because in years to come people who look back on the decision taken now may find
[The Chairman.]
the background to it in the minister's address. On that occasion he said:
I read with great interest the objective of your association as it appears in summary form in the 1966 directory.
"The objective of the association, with full recognition of the interests of the consuming public and the general welfare and security of the nation, shall be to conduct research studies on such matters as costs, supply and demand, foreign trade, productive capacity, and secondary recovery; to provide information on economic trends and national policies affecting oil and gas production; and to advance the welfare of the domestic petroleum industry in the United States, to the end that the nation may be assured of adequate oil and gas supplies for our expanding economy and national security."
I want to draw particular attention to the next sentence in the minister's address, having in mind that this organization was established to look after the interests of the United States regarding oil. The minister went on to say:
I am tempted to suggest that with a simple addition of "and Canada" to the words "United States", we would be all set with a good bipartite institution!
Then he went on to say:
However, we do not have to await such a development in order to allow things Canadian to receive full and sympathetic consideration with the I.P.A.A.
It is interesting to note that the releases from Washington today by the federal power commission have absolutely nothing to do with whether or not the Great Lakes project is a good project but simply with whether it is in the interests of the United States, particularly the national security of the United States. One of the press releases says that the commission's decision also touched on a significant point in respect of future Canadian natural gas and crude oil exports to the United States. It did so in referring to United States national security and the importance of safe reserves of petroleum.
In other words, it does not matter about Canada. All that matters is whether the national security of the United States is protected because they got the hell scared out of them in the Middle East during the last few weeks. Now they have decided that their national interest overrides any consideration that the federal power commission previously had been discussing. In this connection it is interesting to note that last year the minister said:
I am tempted to suggest that with a simple addition of "and Canada" to the words "United States", we would be all set with a good bipartite institution!
June 20, 1967

If that is not continentalism a la Liberal party philosophy then I am surprised.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF ENERGY, MINES AND RESOURCES
speechtext: Is the implication of what my hon. friend is saying that we will always, systematically and unavoidably, have opposition between the United States and Canada? Are there not times when the interests of both countries could run along the same lines?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF ENERGY, MINES AND RESOURCES
speechtext: I think in the main they do, and I think they can. I am not disagreeing with that statement, but I point out that in his address last October he quoted the objective of the Independent Petroleum Association which was established to protect American markets and national security in that country. To that objective the minister would add "and Canada," which carries the implication that we are not going to worry about Canadian national security and Canadian needs but are going to throw our reserves behind the United States which will then be in a much better position to protect its national interests, and I am sure the minister will agree they are not necessarily our interests.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF ENERGY, MINES AND RESOURCES
speechtext: If I may make one comment, I promise never to try to be humorous from now on. I was speaking to the Independent Petroleum Association of America. This association is traditionally opposed to Canadian exports to the United States. I was trying to demonstrate that the purpose of their institution could also be the purpose of Canada, and the humorous implication was better received in Dallas than it seems to have been received in this chamber this afternoon.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF ENERGY, MINES AND RESOURCES
speechtext:
The minister may be right. I have read the full text of his address, and he went on to say that Norman Chappell had been trying to work out an oil policy in such a way that it would be in the interests of both parties. My position is a very simple one, and this is why I am so violently critical of the decisions of the National Energy Board. Its decisions should be designed to cater to the needs of Canada and the foreseeable requirements of Canadian markets. The fact that we are in a very serious bind with respect to gas supplies this year is an indication that the National Energy Board either failed in its duty to protect our national interests by projecting far enough ahead the position that Canada should take or, worse than that, it has not had the authority or the power to influence to any extent the planning of Trans-Canada.
Supply-Energy, Mines and Resources
I have carefully read the position taken by Northern and Central in Ontario as set out by Mr. Bovey, president of that company. He has stated that we will be short 20 billion to 33 billion cubic feet of gas this year. I am sure the minister is aware of the fact that no matter what we do in Canada there would be some economic advantage in exporting gas to parts of the United States and in importing gas into Canada in other areas. I am sure he is also aware that the economics of our gas industry are interrelated between the United States and Canada.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
In respect of Mr. Bovey wanting to go into the Montreal market, I spoke to him the other day and indicated that in my opinion he was as bad as the National Energy Board in his estimates because at the present time there is a 16-inch line I believe, between Ottawa and Montreal to supply that market. The market in Montreal is totally untapped. It can probably be estimated for a matter of two or three years by taking into consideration the market in Toronto and applying that figure to Montreal. In three years the market in Montreal can probably be as great as that in Toronto today. Therefore, to speak of a 30-inch line in Canada, as has been suggested by Trans-Canada, is unrealistic. It is also unrealistic for the National Energy Board to allow the company to consider a 30-inch line.
It is totally unrealistic to speak in these terms particularly when we are dealing with approximately 67 million cubic feet of gas and in five years, in order to make this project economic, will be exporting to the United States up to 500 million cubic feet of gas. Really we are bringing 200 million cubic feet of gas into Canada which is insignificant in respect of the needs of today when there is an immediate shortage of 20 billion to 33 billion cubic feet this year. If we are talking about going into the market in Montreal and the demand for the foreseeable future, we should be talking probably of a 60 or 70-inch line.
I asked Mr. Bovey why this had not been considered. He said that he had just recently returned from an international conference where the representatives of most of the countries had said that this was impractical. He said that they would not be able to handle this kind of a line and that most companies could not make it. I telephoned the Algoma Steel Corporation and was advised that they make plate up to 14 feet which would give something in the order of a 57 or 58-inch line. Such a line has not been built on the North
1720	COMMONS
Supply-Energy, Mines and Resources American continent to date but we in Canada can conceive of a foreseable need for it.
Mr. Bovey told me that at the international conference which he attended he was advised by the Russian representative that Russia is in the process of providing the facilities for a pipe line which will be 100 inches in diameter. A 100-inch pipe line would probably be 20 or 30 times the size of the largest pipe line we have in Canada at the present time. I would think it would be able to operate on low pressure and could be installed economically with a view to meeting the needs 20 years from now.
The minister may be unaware of some of the things which happen when a pipe line is built. There is a very great degree of disruption no matter where the pipe line goes so far as the people are concerned. I remember a farmer in my area who said that he did not care if they paid him a million dollars. He said he did not want it going anywhere near his barn because it might blow up. If the minister would like to know the facts, we stopped them building the pipe line on that particular farm. They had to move the Trans-Canada line over one mile in order to find another place to build the pipe line. This person was able to stop it because he had a D.V.A. loan and the government itself was interested in protecting him.
The government should be looking ahead five, ten or 15 years. Trans-Canada has no money. I do not think it has a very good opportunity to raise money. Its stock is not very high, its dividends are low and it is going to have difficulty raising money. If it is going to instal a major gas transmission line the government likely will have to help in the development. We did this in 1956. We put up the money for the northern section. It was very difficult country in which to build and we allowed the Trans-Canada a ten year period in which to operate line, take the profit out of it, and then buy it at its original cost. This is a fairly lucrative way of constructing a pipe line.
If the war in the Middle East had not happened I am sure the minister would have had to come to parliament and ask for assistance to construct part of this line in order to meet the needs of eastern Canada. I have no objection to his asking parliament for such assistance. I would think, however, that there are very few companies which are less deserving of receiving help than this company. They have played cat and mouse with the Canadian government and even worse with

DEBATES	June 20, 1967
the Canadian people. But I think the Canadian government would have had to put up at least $200 million to put in the necessary loop in northwestern Ontario.
This is a company which is not respecting the monopoly we have given it. It is a monopoly which I do not believe it is the responsibility of the government to supervise but rather that of the agency we have established, the National Energy Board. The National Energy Board has totally failed in its responsibility in this and in other respects.
I do not know where the 100-inch pipeline to which Mr. Bovey referred is going to be or whether it is for gas or oil, but I presume if they are going to use 100-inch pipe it will be for a transmission line from their oil fields to the take-off point for their distribution line and that the line probably will not be utilized to capacity for some time. It seems odd that Trans-Canada is raising more money now to increase the capacity of a facility they finished less than ten years ago. It seems to me it is very poor engineering when you have long term debentures on a capital investment such as a pipe line that will not meet the supply requirements for the next 20 years to cover the period of the debentures.
I do not know whether the minister is happy about the fact that this matter now appears to have been settled. I have made inquiries of one of the interested parties and have asked whether the intention is to go through the court procedure. I understand that in the United States the court procedure has already been tested to some degree in this regard. Let me read a paragraph from the business and financial section of the Globe and Mail for May 25, 1967:
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
Panhandle's application for renewed hearings of the Great Lakes scheme may well be rejected by the commission but such a ruling by the F.P.C. would almost certainly be cited by the company as one of its grounds for challenging the legality of any F.P.C. decision in favour of Great Lakes if Panhandle resolves to take it to the courts.
I understand other companies are interested in testing such a decision in the courts, and I wonder what position Trans-Canada would be in in respect of the work it might do if an injunction were obtained. I have no idea what the company intends to do in the next few weeks but if it does anything it will be in a ridiculous position should an injunction be granted. It might be in an even more ridiculous position that it would be if it waited four or five months to see what decision might be made.
June 20, 1S67	COMMONS DEBATES	1721
This whole situation leaves Canada with very little protection. I am sure the minister is not so callous in his regard for Canadian interests as to allow a situation to continue as a result of which we must depend on the whims of the federal power commission or the United States courts. Everyone is agreed that gas is not going to be made available this year from this project, but I am interested in this line going through my area of northern Ontario in 1968 or 1969. The hon. member for Timmins said that he does not care whether the line is built along old highway number 11 or highway 17 through Sault Ste. Marie. We do not have a real preference in this regard, but the minister must consider the fact that organized townships in the farming area of northern Ontario depend on the pipe line for 50 per cent of their assessment revenue. This may not be of great concern to the department but it is of great concern to these townships and municipalities because they require this tax revenue to provide education and other necessary services. If this line is not constructed along highway 17 or highway 11 the loss in tax revenue will amount to hundreds of millions of dollars, and there will be a tremendous loss so far as construction employment opportunities are concerned.
I am not worried at all about the minister's position or whether the United States and Canada should pool their resources to meet the needs of this continent in the most economical way possible, but I think I would be a very poor citizen of the United States if I was not more concerned about the national economy of that country than whether or not the people of Iran have another slice of bread on their tables. The people of the United States seem to look at Canada in the same way they look at the Near East, as a reservoir of potential resources for their personal use and economic advantage.
It is not my concern that the National Energy Board or the government should decide how much of a reserve we must have in Canada, how much gas should be delivered to Canadian markets and how much exported. I was surprised at what the hon. member for Qu'Appelle said, and I usually have a very high respect for his opinions. In this regard he has been playing a very narrow and restricted game. In Sudbury he said he was the only one interested in having the line go through Sudbury. He has also said that his interest is in the economics of the routes through southern Ontario. He is interested in reducing the cost to that part of the province.
Supply-Energy, Mines and Resources
Various members from Alberta have been very clear in their position. They say that we have a surplus of gas and should sell it. They apparently do not care where we sell it as long as we do. I am not sure that I would not have a similar view if I came from that part of the country and knew there was a surplus of this saleable commodity. I think I would also want to sell it. Apparently the Alberta members do not care a damn who gets the commodity.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF ENERGY, MINES AND RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, just to clarify what has been said, let me point out that the members from Alberta have been consistent in their position so far as gas is concerned in that Alberta should be considered first, then Canada and then the export markets. They have never said they do not give a damn who gets it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF ENERGY, MINES AND RESOURCES
speechtext:
I stand corrected. Perhaps that was my interpretation of what I heard. Apparently I am not in disagreement with the hon. member for Medicine Hat who says that Alberta's needs must be considered first. All of us here have a political responsibility in representing different ridings. Leaving aside my interest in the particular area of the country which I represent and leaving aside the regional economic interests of other hon. members, it seems to me that whenever Trans-Canada says that more gas must be exported to the United States market to make the proposition feasible it is expressing a pipe line interest and not necessarily a Canadian interest. Surely this is a public commodity which is in the hands of one private operator. I have sometimes felt that there should be more than one operator in this field. However, one must remember what has happened to our transportation system as a result of the operation of the Canadian National and Canadian Pacific railways.
I believe that the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources should make an assessment of our needs for the next 25 years and adopt a policy which will ensure that they will be met. Perhaps that department should put up the money to operate such a venture. Perhaps we should have a crown corporation to operate a pipe line company. If everybody is sold on the idea of another line, let us see that the money is raised and the line built so that all areas of the country can have the advantage of this commodity.
I do not think the Canadian people are going to be satisfied with the decision that has now been made by the federal power commission. That decision was made in the interests
June 20. 1967
1722	COMMONS
Supply-Energy, Mines and Resources of United States security because of the Middle East situation. I think we will eventually have to do what was suggested originally, build a line that will serve the needs of the Canadian people rather than primarily export needs. In other words, we must meet Canadian needs not only in the foreseeable future but for as long as it is feasible to project such needs. I have talked to a member of the house who probably has more experience in this regard than anybody sitting in the gallery. He says it is quite possible to project the potential of the wells and the potential of the fields. He says that this kind of projection can be made, and in my opinion it is the only kind of projection that will satisfy the Canadian public.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there are two things I should like to bring to the attention of the minister. One is the pollution of the St. Croix river and basin. I know the minister is aware of this problem because I have received from his office copies of papers concerning the Saint John and St. Croix international river basin. The buck has been passed around for a good many years in respect of solving the pollution of this basin.
It has been possible to pass the buck around in this way because so many people are interested in the question. They include the International Joint Commission, the state of Maine, the federal government of the U.S.A., Calais, Maine, Milltown, Maine, Milltown, New Brunswick, St. Stephen, New Brunswick, the federal government of Canada, the province of New Brunswick, the fisheries department, and the Georgia Pacific Company.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF ENERGY, MINES AND RESOURCES
speechtext: All aboard.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF ENERGY, MINES AND RESOURCES
speechtext:
This basin is so polluted and the sludge is so thick on the banks of the river that if you paint a house white it is black or grey the next morning. This actually happens. It has been going on for years. The buck has been passed around not only in Canada but in the United States. I have before me a copy of a letter written by the water improvement commission of Maine which says:
As you know the Maine Water Improvement Commission submitted a bill to the 1963 legislature which was intended to give it the necessary power to require pollution abatement on international boundary streams such as the St. Croix river and
[Mr. Peters.)

portions of the St. John river. This was, for some reason never explained to the Water Improvement Commission, labelled unconstitutional by the attorney general and withdrawn from committee.
All of this left enforcement of any program strictly up to the federal agency, as the hearing commitee of the 1965 legislature to whom the bill was resubmitted gave it no consideration on the grounds that it would interfere with pending lederal legislation.
There was no federal legislation passed in this respect, and the pollution goes on and on. Some companies manufacturing food products in St. Stephen even claim that the fumes from the river basin are affecting their products. Somebody must take the lead in straightening out this matter. I think the minister is the man to do this. He could take the lead in this respect and see that the basin is cleaned out. I have here a copy of a letter written by John S. Bates, chairman of the New Brunswick water authority, who says:
The New Brunswick water authority looks on the accumulation of sludge banks between St. Stephen and Calais as a large-scale result of pollution by solids and solubles from Woodland-
That is the Georgia Pacific mill. I attended a meeting with the Georgia Pacific company and others at which this problem was discussed. They have done something about it but the money for what was done was in the main supplied by the federal government of the United States of America. However, the pollution continues. This was a great salmon stream at one time. The salmon come up a short way and die, so the fisheries department should be interested in the problem. They are interested in it, but somebody must take the lead. I hope the minister will look into the problem and do something about it.
There is another matter I should like to bring to the attention of the minister. He is minister of mines and must be interested in the gold mines of Canada. At one time gold was the metal that brought us in more money than any other metal. However, we are now paying the gold mines $15 an ounce when the price used to be $35 an ounce. We were paying the gold mines $35 an ounce in 1934 and now, because of the decrease in the purchasing power of the dollar, we are paying them $15 an ounce. The governor of the Bank of Canada has indicated that gold is not only a monetary measure but is a commodity. Can the minister point to any commodity in Canada which had such a price in 1934 and where the price is now down to less than half? I think this situation is ridiculous. Further, the taxpayers of Canada are paying subsidies to the gold mines to get the gold out

of the ground. Last year we paid subsidies of something like $2,500,000 to a syndicate of Americans.
The Americans cannot buy our centennial gold pieces; they cannot buy our gold at all. But they can come up here and take over our gold mines. They do this by taking over one mine, stopping the dividends, taking the treasury, buying another mine, and so on. At the present time they own about 18 gold mines in this country. To this syndicate the government paid subsidies which last year amounted to $2,500,000. What happened to the gold? After we paid the Americans $2,500,000 to get it out of the ground, we sold the gold to the United States government for $35 an ounce. It probably cost us $45 or $50 an ounce to get the gold out of the ground. In my opinion this is an extremely silly policy and the minister should look into it. If we were getting the right price for our gold, instead of receiving $140 million we should be receiving $500 million or $600 million a year.
There is gold from coast to coast in this country. All we need to do is to dig it out of the ground in order to get international liquidity. Liquidity is required now in international monetary affairs. I understand that nine out of the "big ten" want to raise the price of gold in order to obtain liquidity.
I read a book by Sir Roy Harrod, the British economist who was adviser to Lord Keynes when we signed the Bretton Woods agreement agreeing to pay only $35 an ounce forever to our gold mines. We signed this agreement. Sir Roy Harrod said in his book that the International Monetary Fund certainly had to be revised and reorganized and the only way to do it was to double the price of gold as a preliminary and increase the drawing rights of the members. I understand the United States agreed to increase the drawing rights but refused and still refuses to increase the price of gold. In my opinion to do so would be to their benefit and it would certainly be to the benefit of Canada.
I hope the minister will look into this problem. He is minister of mines and should be interested in gold as well as other metals. It was once our most valuable metal and could still be our most valuable metal if the price was right.

Mr. Chairman, I want to go back to the subject of the decision announced today by the federal power commission and raised in the house by the hon. member for Timmins and the hon. member for Timis-kaming. My version of what happened at
Supply-Energy, Mines and Resources eleven o'clock this morning is quite different from the version of the two N.D.P. members. I believe this decision by the federal power commission of the United States is a great day for Canada. I want to state my reasons very clearly for saying this. It is a great day for Canada, it is a great day for northern Ontario, it is a great day for Quebec and it is a great day for the west. My only complaint about the decision announced today, June 20, 1967, is that it should have been reached a year ago. If it had not been for the cowardice of the present government it would have been reached last year, e (4:00 p.m.)
Last year the Alberta Conservation Board agreed that they had surplus gas. The National Energy Board recommended the acceptance of the Great Lakes application to the government, but for some reason which we will never know for certain the government turned down that recommendation. When some of us opposed that decision and gave our reasons for our opposition to a decision which we understood to be a purely political one brought about on the basis of the N.D.P. opposition in northern Ontario, the government changed its mind after a couple of months and agreed to the application. This gave our economic foes in the United States a new breath of life and they renewed their objections to the application under due process of law before the federal power commission. As a result there has been a long delay this year which has cost the consumers of central Canada large sums of money, has hurt the producers in western Canada, and has given a temporary additional market in Canada to the United States pipe lines.
The other day I suggested to the minister something which I thought should have been done last year. I said to him that the United States government should have been asked to request their court of record, the federal power commission, to expedite the proceedings of this hearing. There are many precedents for such a request, and I think our country should have thrown its weight behind the Canadian company which was battling for a Canadian market. I put this on the record last fall and I repeat it today. Who was opposed to this application? The United States coal companies were opposed because in the application they saw a loss of Canadian markets for United States coal. Likewise the unions of the coal companies were opposed for the same reason. The oil companies of the United States were also opposed to it because they saw a
June 20, 1967
1724	COMMONS
Supply*-Energy, Mines and Resources loss of markets in this area, and so were the gas pipe line companies in the United States. Several of the states in the United States were also opposed. All these groups were fighting on behalf of the United States economy. We cannot blame them for doing so, but when I listened in the house to Canadians joining the Americans to take away a Canadian market from Canadians I asked myself, who is the real Canadian?
The government does not have a leg to stand on. They wobbled, they twisted, but no one fought for Canadians. The essential fact of this proposal is that an economical looping of the pipe line will not only bring about the establishment of the shortest route in terms of capital cost but will also provide advantages because of the storage provisions in Ontario and in Michigan which would give us a high load factor and thus would reduce the wholesale price. Last fall I stated that by building the loop through the United States we would reduce the price for the industrial markets in Ontario and Quebec by approximately 15 per cent. For the first time gas prices in Ontario would be lower than they are across the border in the United States, and every person with half an ounce of brain knows what this means. It means that our cost of manufacturing would be lower than that of the United States, and when companies are planning future expansion of their business, whether it be in steel or any secondary industry, they naturally know where the costs are lower. Instead of building plants in Buffalo and Detroit they will go where the price is lower in Windsor, Hamilton or Toronto. This is the key fact.
The charge which has been made that we have lost control is nothing more than an innuedo because 50 per cent of the ownership belongs to the Canadian company and it is they who control it as long as they obey the laws laid down by the F.P.C. In the original application 90 per cent of the gas was to come from western to eastern Canada and only 10 per cent was to be dropped off in the towns along the way. So I have no choice but to say again in the house that the position of the N.D.P. has been harmful to every portion of Ontario and Quebec where natural gas is being used. It is the N.D.P. who have stood in the path of the development of the wealth of this country through the use of this great natural resource. In my eyes, and I hope in the eyes of all the people of Canada, they stand condemned for this selfish and outdated nationalistic approach.


I am aware of their arguments and I know how much these northern townships depend on the construction of a pipe line in their area. I know from personal experience how the motel operators and the people who run hotels and restaurants depend on new construction in their area. I say now to the N.D.P. that not only will the people of Windsor, Toronto, London, Hamilton and Montreal get cheaper gas as a result of the decision announced today by the F.P.C. but so will all of northern Ontario. Furthermore, very shortly northern Ontario will get a second pipe line and all the benefits that will accrue from it. Their motels will be filled and their assessment will be raised. They will have the best of two worlds. We have saved the Canadian market for Canadian products. We have not raised artificial barriers to save that market but we have achieved our purpose in a positive and economic way.
I also said that northern Canada would benefit for another reason and that is that more gas will be available this coming winter as a result of the decision announced today. In the last couple of years several companies and mills in northern Ontario had been short of natural gas. Whether we like it or not, the premium markets are in the big cities. With permission for the looping now having been given, this coming summer we will be able to hook up our storage fields near Sarnia in Lambton county to the storage fields in Michigan to supply the Ontario market. In this way more gas can be made available to the northern towns, mills and companies this winter. This is a great day for northern Ontario which will get more gas this winter, and when the loop is completed next year the gas will be cheaper. I say this is true, modern Canadianism, not the artificial restrictive nationalism which should have died in our country 40 years ago.
I have put these thoughts on the record because I believe them to be vital to the whole concept I have, and which I hope many Canadians have, of building our nation. We want to build it on the basis of positive, non-restrictive techniques. We have the basic resources, we have the energy and we have the water with which we can process in Canada so much more cheaply than any other country in the world. We should realize that this is a heaven-sent situation and that at long last we are able to achieve what we want in an economic way. We do not want to impose any restrictions on the Americans; we just want to do things better and cheaper.
June 20. 1967

I know that the large American gas companies in Louisiana and Texas want the market in Ontario and Quebec. It is a good market for the future. But at least this once we have won a victory. Our Canadian gas is just as good as the gas from Louisiana. Without the need for any subsidy from the government or any artificial restrictions we are able to reduce the price of gas below the United States price through the use of the storage facilities in Lambton county in Ontario and in Michigan. We are able to do in a positive way what we have tried to do in the past by using restrictive techniques. This is a good day for Canada.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
I agree with my hon. friend from Timis-kaming that we as legislators should have been better informed about the sudden rise in the market in Ontario and Quebec two years ago. The crisis of the last 18 months should not have been allowed to develop. I hope that the words of the hon. member for Timis-kaming will be listened to and that an effort will be made to make some projections. Whether they be optimistic, pessimistic or mean projections, let us make some projections so that we can assess whether the needs of the consumer will be met. It is true that we have chosen this company as the instrument of the Canadian people to move gas from western to eastern Canada. But in giving this company a charter we have a responsibility to see that they meet their commitments. I believe that they can do the job better and at cheaper cost than a crown corporation or any kind of government organization, but we do need advice from the National Energy Board in regard to future demand for gas.
I said, Mr. Chairman, that this was a great day for Quebec. Those of us who have travelled through the province of Quebec realize the desperate need in Canada's interest for a greater variety of industrial activity to improve the economic health of that province. One of the things which has been denied the areas outside Montreal is access to natural gas. With the price reduction which will arise from this loop I see the wholesale price in Montreal going down to the point where we can now consider building a line from Montreal through the southern townships to Quebec city and later perhaps along the north shore to Quebec city. This will give those 20 or 30 counties access to a clean, efficient fuel which is particularly suited to modern types of precision operated industry.

I know that a pipe line to Quebec city is going to run in the red for a few years and that under the old price structure which obtained it was impossible to build the line. But I hope that there is now a chance for the people living in the heavily populated rural areas between Montreal and Quebec city, both on the north shore and the south shore, to have the opportunity to benefit from the type of industry which will complement their agricultural activities. It will be a great day for Quebec if all of these things materialize, and I know they will.
I think I have said enough, Mr. Chairman, to make my position clear, but I still want to offer one or two words of advice to the minister. One of the important principles enshrined in the National Energy Board Act is the common carrier principle. In plain terms this means that all producers of gas have an equal right to pump their gas through a line and that all consumers have an equal right to buy their gas from the owners of that line. But it also means that price must vary with distance from the source, and this is extremely important in Canada. For example, if gas goes to the United States it is very important to realize that the common carrier principle of pricing the gas more cheaply closer to the source must be maintained.
I realize that the volume argument also comes into the picture. It is argued that if you take a large volume you should pay a lower price for it. However, I share with some of my friends in the N.D.P. this concern: If we want to build a better Canada, one of the ways we have to make certain that the national interest is protected is to see that the common carrier principle is maintained.
Second, Mr. Chairman, we have learned a lesson from the experience last year, and that is that Canada and the United States will increasingly have to work together to find a solution to our common energy needs. I think the principle should be that the consumer has the greatest right to the cheapest possible form of energy. Perhaps I should explain that first principle a little more. To make sure that the consumer is protected we should always supply gas at the most economical price. In other words, we do not just distribute it all around so as to maintain a supply in Canada or the United States. The most economic price and the shortest possible route is the end objective from the consumer point of view.
The second principle is that the Canadian interest must be protected too. I think that the Canadian interest can be maintained by realizing that under the terms of the National

Supply-Energy, Mines and Resources Energy Board Act, which lays down various criteria which must be applied when a company is going to build or operate a pipe line, the National Energy Board can be used as a sort of bargaining agent both on behalf of companies and on behalf of provinces which own the gas. This concept has been put forward very ably by a member on the government benches, the hon. member for Coast-Capilano. I should like to see a public statement made by the minister in the form of a directive to the National Energy Board, in cases where a company is sending gas to the United States and is perhaps fighting for the big markets of North America, saying that in the bargaining the competitive price of other fuels in the areas in which the fuel is to be sold will be taken into consideration. In other words, it is not just a question of selling the maximum amount of gas possible; it is a matter of getting the maximum return for our resources.
Many of us, Mr. Chairman, have the suspicion that much of our resources which are owned by subsidiaries of United States companies return a very small emolument per unit sold, that the main profit on natural resources in Canada goes to the parent company in the United States which finally uses the product. Once again I compliment the hon. member for Coast-Capilano for bringing out evidence of this nature. I think this is the type of matter in which the National Energy Board should take an interest.
If I may go back to my first statement about this latter subject, we have learned the lesson in the last year that if we have to deal more and more with the United States there should be a meeting between the federal power commission and the National Energy Board, both in effect being courts of record, to lay down the terms of reference with regard to future across the border applications.
I accept the right of every American to due process of law in United States courts. But I also want to protect the right of every Canadian to make certain that Canadian resources do not become the tool of a foreign court. Because of the mutual interest of the United States in having access, even at a higher price, to our resources in Canada, terms of reference laying down how applications shall be heard in future will prevent the kind of long delays that have been taking place.
If as a result of this meeting, Mr. Chairman, an understanding were reached on the principle that we are entitled to the maximum


price that the market will allow for our products, the United States will have to accept that because the terms of bargaining are on our side. All of the reports and forecasts indicate the need for more energy as the years go by, and the National Energy Board is the agency that can protect us. However, the terms of the act of today would have to be enlarged.
In the meantime the situation requires a statement on the part of the responsible minister, speaking on behalf of the people of Canada, in the form of a directive to the National Energy Board. This was the technique which was used in connection with our national oil policy, and even though I am not going to speak today about that policy I would point out that this precedent could be applied to a natural gas policy. In this regard, Mr. Chairman, we sorely lack direction. Let the minister take all the time he requires to work out the terms of reference, but the United States should be told that we are giving our energy board this directive. Then the two energy bodies could work together to ensure that the right of Americans to due process of their law is not taken away from them, particularly in cases of border convenience, but that we in Canada should not be asked to continue to suffer the delays which have occurred during the last year.

Mr. Chairman, on Wednesday last I began to make some remarks with respect to the Nelson river project and how it affects Canadian industry, particularly the Canadian General Electric Company. I spoke of the opportunities which national resource development on this scale provides for our country. I should like to complete the remarks I was making on that day.
The point I was making when I was interrupted was that major projects such as the Nelson river project provide an opportunity for Canadian industry and, indeed, for foreign industry, to develop technology, to increase employment and to explore export potentials. I suggested it is imperative, when a decision is made as to who should undertake the work, that consideration go beyond the mere question of cost. Decisions of this character must be founded on a much broader basis than an inquiry as to which bid happens to be lowest.
We have a device which is used in this country as a measure of protection to ensure that Canadian content is taken into consideration when awarding such contracts. It is known as the 10 per cent formula and it may or may not be adequate. It seems to me that when making an assessment as to its adequacy this formula has to be examined in comparison with similar devices or formulae used by other countries. It would be a useful venture for the Department of Industry or the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources to examine the conditions faced by the Canadian General Electric Company, for example, in bidding for contracts in Sweden, France or the United Kingdom. With such a study we could discover exactly what form of protection exists in those countries for their own industries.

If we were to undertake such an investigation we might find that our 10 per cent formula affords much less protection to Canadian industry than do comparable formulae or devices used by other countries. It is important when we are considering developments of this magnitude, the Nelson river project, for example, in which Canadian industry is likely to be competing with British or Swedish industry, that Canadian industry on its own ground should be in a no less favourable competitive position than it is when competing for contracts in these other countries. If this is not the case it should be the case, and we should take measures to make sure that Canadian industry is not exposed at home to greater competition than are indigenous industries in other countries. Since the Nelson river project can have an important bearing on the development of Canadian technology, on employment and on export sales, it is important that we give this matter urgent attention.
The federal government has decided to invest a large sum of money in the Nelson river project. This investment takes the form of building the transmission line, together with its associated terminal equipment, to make it possible for the Manitoba Hydro-Electric Board to develop the resources of the Nelson river in northern Manitoba to supply the power requirements of Manitoba and Saskatchewan and to create an opportunity to export power to the United States.
Atomic Energy of Canada Limited has been appointed by the federal government to design and purchase the equipment for this major transmission system. It has selected a relatively new technique, high voltage direct current, as being the most economic and efficient means to bring this power south to the area of need.
All of the high voltage direct current systems built or being built to date use mercury arc valves as the main element in the terminals. New developments, however, in semiconductor materials, and their successful displacement of mercury arc valves in industrial applicants, suggest that they would bring the same benefits to this installation as they have to industrial users.
Canada is fortunate that this semi-conductor technology has progressed to the point where it can utilize this equipment on its first major high voltage direct current installation. It gives Canada the opportunity to lead the world in this field.
A prototype equipment has been built and proven. Canadian General Electric has anticipated this development by training people

Supply-Energy, Mines and Resources in the special requirements of electric utility applications, and also in building and installing systems using this same basic technology. Through its role in the Nelson river transmission project, and by purchasing the necessary equipment in Canada, the federal government has a wonderful opportunity in my view to achieve a number of important goals. By using Canadian equipment it would help to create employment in Canada. It would support and expand Canadian manufacturing capability and, above all, establish its manufacturing industry in a strong technological leadership position. This technological ability is necessary not only to supply our future domestic requirements but also to create opportunities for export.

In the decision that has to be made, and will be made by the Atomic Energy Commission, it is important to remember that the Canadian General Electric Company's proposal will have a Canadian content many times that of any other manufacturer, whether domestic or foreign. It is estimated that placing the contract with this company would probably result in 700 man-years of employment in design, manufacture and installation of the equipment involved, and would in effect create a new industry of considerable size which in turn would provide a livelihood for a considerable number of people in the trades, professions and the service industries.
In a decision on this matter it is well to bear in mind that the company I have mentioned has already made a large investment in developing the necessary skills, research and development programs, and the building of prototypes to prove out the technology involved. Without a contract to supply the equipment and services required this investment would be lost. More important, the technology would not be further developed and the technical and manufacturing leadership would have to remain with foreign manufacturers who would, of course, continue to supply both Canadian and world-wide requirements for high voltage direct current transmission for years to come.
For these reasons, Mr. Chairman, my submission today is brief and absolutely straightforward. It seems to me in a project of this magnitude that Atomic Energy of Canada Limited and the government of Canada have a very important decision to make which should be based in the final analysis on a

Mr. Chairman, I wish to deal briefly this afternoon with one specific project referred to by the minister in his introductory statement on Wednesday, June 14, found at page 1521 of Hansard. Part of the sentence in question reads:
-and we are negotiating with British Columbia a joint program for flood abatement in the lower Fraser valley.
I have indicated that my remarks are going to be brief but I hope no one is going to assume that because they are brief my concern is slight. I believe this is one of the most urgent problems that require attention in the Fraser valley because it affects the entire lower mainland of the province of British Columbia.
Although we in the lower Fraser valley hope that the immediate danger has passed for this year, the area annualy faces the danger of flood and disaster. In referring to natural catastrophes the explanation is often given that they are acts of God. Since it appears that we are being spared a repetition of flood conditions such as we had in 1948, in all fairness we ought to give credit to God who has to take the blame for many of the unfortunate situations that happen.
The problems we face in the lower Fraser valley are mainly occasioned by the sudden spring run-offs in the Fraser River watershed. Each year a careful assessment is made of the varying situations, the gauges on the river are watched very closely, predictions are made and warnings are issued, but the whole situation depends on the weather conditions prevailing at the period of the year when the run-offs take place.
This year in British Columbia we had a combination of conditions which made many people believe we would have a really serious flood situation. I remember speaking to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development on one occasion and he felt that everything was just ideal, if one can use that term, for a really serious flood to develop in the lower Fraser valley. As I say, it now
June 20. 1967

appears that that danger has receded. Nevertheless, as the situation developed emergency plans were made and machinery was put into operation to meet the possible danger.
In the absence of an adequate agreement between the federal and provincial governments, the provincial authorities authorized emergency work on portions of the diking systems along the Fraser valley. We hope that federal assistance will be forthcoming to assist in meeting the financial outlay that was involved.
Hon. members will recall that on various occasions questions have been asked on orders of the day with respect to the situation on the Fraser River and in the Fraser River valley. Those questions were posed by myself and by members of other parties who were just as concerned and as interested as I was. We had the assurance that the federal government was prepared to render every possible assistance should an emergency arise. We appreciated that, but the point I want to make this afternoon is that even though we may appreciate the emergency plans that were in preparation and in readiness, it is going to take something more to satisfy the municipal authorities and the people of the affected areas in British Columbia.
Every year there is a great fear of what might happen, the inconvenience, the loss, even loss of life that might happen should the Fraser River overflow its banks and flood the lower Fraser valley. I was advised by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources that discussions were taking place between the provincial and federal authorities with respect to a long-term plan to eliminate this flood hazard and danger. It was my understanding that a tentative agreement had been reached with respect to the strengthening of the dikes and that consideration was being given to the implementation of the recommendations of the Fraser River Board, which were tabled in September, 1963. I should like to refer briefly to those recommendations but first I should like to read a very brief paragraph from the introduction to the report. It reads as follows:

I wish to point out that this document is dated September, 1963. Of course, we are now approaching September of 1967. What disturbs the people of my constituency and other constituencies which are involved in this problem is that in spite of the potential dangers it seems that nothing is being done to implement the long-term recommendations of the Fraser River Board. It is true that some work is being done on the dikes in the lower Fraser valley, and we appreciate this. I have been given to understand that in this regard they have reached a relatively high degree of efficiency and effectiveness.
I am advised by those who I believe understand the situation much better than I do that the work being done in the lower Fraser valley will not meet the need. They say that the only thing which will meet the need, solve the problem and eliminate the flood danger is the construction of reservoirs in the upper reaches of the Fraser River. These reservoirs would control the flow and enable it to be released slowly in order that it could be carried away. In view of the fact that the recommendations suggest it is an urgent matter, in view of the fact that the authorities and others in the Fraser valley say it is an urgent matter and in view of the fact that we have been presenting these recommendations for some years now, I earnestly request the minister to do his utmost to get the whole proposal and program under way. I realize, of course, that it is not his responsibility alone. The provincial authorities also have a responsibility. What I say to the minister I say also to the provincial government of British Columbia, namely, I hope that action will be taken immediately to implement these recommendations which I have been given to understand offer the only means by which the flood danger in the Fraser valley can be eliminated.
The suggestion has been made that this will be an extremely expensive proposition. Let me say that the implementation of the recommendations, although costly, will not be as costly as the damage and loss which could be experienced if another serious flood should occur in the Fraser valley. Therefore, on behalf of the people of British Columbia and the lower mainland in particular I appeal to the minister again to assist in expediting this program. If he will do this, he will have the appreciation of all those who are concerned about this problem.

On more than one occasion, Mr. Chairman, I have spoken in this house about the illegal filling of Lake Ontario, usually I have done so on the estimates of the Department of Public Works. During the past year I have noted there have been reports in the press and on radio and television that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources has been issuing assurances that he is going to devote a great deal of attention to the question of pollution. Within the last several months I have seen a letter-I have no other authority than that -to the effect that the Department of Transport will be looking after the enforcement of the Navigable Waters Protection Act which has been under the Minister of Public Works for the past few years.
I know that members of the cabinet talk about wanting to have a bill passed by the house relating to the Navigable Waters Protection Act. I suppose it will be a piece of legislation which will give authority to the Minister of Transport. As a private member I am told nothing and have to look to the newspapers to find out what is going on. I rather gather that the Minister of Public Works is still the minister responsible for the enforcement of this act, but yet we are told that the Minister of Transport will look after
[Mr. Patterson.J

it in the future. One only wonders when the change will take effect.
To my knowledge the federal government has never at any time taken a firm stand with regard to the illegal filling which goes on along the northern shore of Lake Ontario between the Humber River and Etobicoke Creek. I should like to congratulate the minister sincerely and heartily for the contribution he is making to the Canada Centre. I know the Ontario government is also contributing to this project. This new centre will be about 22 miles from the district I am speaking of on the north shore of Lake Ontario. This should be the first problem that the Canada Centre is asked to investigate by the able minister and his department. Only yesterday afternoon I was walking on some of this illegal fill. I protest particularly in respect of two pieces of fill, one known as the Millgate fill near the mouth of Etobicoke Creek and the other lying to the south of what is known as Humber House, or hotel, or tavern on Lakeshore Boulevard west.
In the Toronto area recently some of the editorial writers for the daily newspapers have made sport of the council of the borough of Etobicoke because the council passed a bylaw in which they referred to the fact that the southern boundary of the borough is the middle line of Lake Ontario. This is an incontrovertible fact. The newspapers have been making sport of the borough council because it passed a bylaw zoning as parklands, open space or green belt all that part of Lake Ontario between the natural shore and the southern boundary which is the centre line of Lake Ontario. I say to this house, Mr. Chairman, that the borough council of Etobicoke had to pass a bylaw of that nature because the federal cabinet has taken no action to enforce the provisions of the Navigable Waters Protection Act.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
The Millgate development over toward the mouth of Etobicoke Creek, to which I have made reference in the past and to which 1 will refer and keep on referring until the cabinet either declares it national park land or orders the fill to be removed by the people who dumped it there-there is authority for such action in the Navigable Waters Protection Act-projects out into Lake Ontario something like 330 feet, which is a full 110 yards, with a width of about 220 feet. This is earth that has been dumped into Lake Ontario. The waves are beating on it and around it and are wearing it down and scattering
June 20, 1967

mud east and west along the shoreline of Lake Ontario.
If the minister wants to see a fine case of pollution all he has to do is go to the point where Etobicoke Creek empties into Lake Ontario. About a quarter of a mile east he will see a prize example of illegal fill which is playing havoc with Len Ford park. It is on the shoreline and belonged originally to the village of Long Branch and now to the borough of Etobicoke which enveloped that village. He will find private owners along this shoreline who are protesting about the mud, the flotsam and the jetsam which is being washed up on the shore three-quarters of a mile east and west of this Millgate fill. Why cannot the minister responsible for pollution get either the Minister of Transport or the Minister of Public Works to enforce that provision of the Navigable Waters Protection Act which says that those who deposit illegal fill without having their plans approved prior to such action will be forced to remove them or the government may remove them and charge the expense of removal to those people who dumpted the illegal fill?
Let us leave the Millgate aspect for a moment and go farther east to the mouth of the Humber River, where I was 24 hours ago. The muddy water extends out into Lake Ontario for half a mile to three-quarters of a mile, and with the wind being from the southeast yesterday the muddy appearance of the water was evident for possibly two to two and a half miles west of the Humber River. If you stand on Lakeshore Boulevard you can count possibly 1,000 dump loads of fill on top of the illegal fill which has been placed there over the years. I say that you can count 1,000 dump loads of fill which have not been levelled off by bulldozers or other mechanical action and are conclusive proof that fill has been brought there and is still being brought there in order that lots can be created in Lake Ontario which will sell for at least $500,000 per acre.
The area of fill south of the Humber hotel is much larger than in the case of the Mill-gate fill farther to the west. It is so large that the people who developed it have even had the effrontery to go before the council of the borough of Etobicoke and ask to have the property zoned for an apartment house and hotel construction. The land that they want zoned by the borough of Etobicoke is created land that did not exist there until they started putting fill in Lake Ontario. It is interesting to note that the borough of Etobicoke recognizes that the land is there and is paying
Supply-Energy, Mines and Resources attention to their demands that an unopened road allowance running from Lakeshore Boulevard down to Lake Ontario shall be closed. These people are illegally filling in Lake Ontario without any obstruction from the Minister of Public Works, or should I say the Minister of Transport, because I do not know who is responsible at the moment. I can only tell the house that neither of them is accepting responsibility. Neither of them has stopped this illegal fill being dumped into Lake Ontario. I am told that the council of the borough of Etobicoke is passing a regulation to close up that street allowance as it would separate the two pieces of fill these people would like to have as one big building lot rather than two small ones, in exchange for a promise that there will be another road allowance provided on the west side of the fill.
What I am drawing to the attention of the chairman and members of the committee is the fact that the federal cabinet simply stands by and does nothing to enforce the Navigable Waters Protection Act. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources stands up and talks about the great action he is going to take to stop pollution, but these people keep dumping mud, fill, broken concrete and cinder blocks into Lake Ontario. Three weeks ago there was fill dumped into the lake at the foot of Thirteenth Street in the former town of New Toronto which is now part of the borough of Etobicoke.
I should like to ask the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources whether he will follow up with action his promises that he is going to stop pollution in Lake Ontario and all other waters that come under his jurisdiction. The people in the south end of the borough of Etobicoke know they cannot expect any action from the Minister of Public Works. He has had years in which to do something but he has done nothing. There may be some hope that the Minister of Transport will do something, but in view of the delay in bringing the Navigable Waters Protection Act under his jurisdiction I felt I should now ask the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources to use his good offices to see that this illegal filling is stopped.
The property that has been created should be turned into national parks for the benefit of all the people, not just some would-be builders. The pollution should be controlled in the interests of all the people on the north shore of Lake Ontario. Anyone flying in or out of Toronto, if their plane flies along the

It stands out like a sore thumb in two or three places where the Department of Public Works does not interfere with the dumping.
In view of the legal connections involved in this illegal fill I can only state that if some cabinet minister does not take the necessary drastic action shortly the cabinet will have more on its hands than it can handle, because all the legal niceties tied up with this illegal All are well known to the people living in the south end of Etobicoke and to the members of the Etobicoke borough council.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to take just a few minutes first of all to present my roses to the minister as a token of my admiration for the way in which he fulfils his obligations. I hope he will accept them, and to make them even more agreeable, I will make them "American Beauty".
Mr. Chairman, in his opening remarks on his estimates, the minister said that water was one of our most important resources. I think that no one questions this statement and we realize it even more when we are somewhat deprived. In fact, that is when we realize that water is of primary importance and that it must be used reasonably, since it is not an inexhaustible resource.
As the minister said, Canada is favoured, because we have a lot of fresh water for our population. If my information is correct, I think Canada owns approximately one fifth of the fresh water in the free world, and the province of Quebec has one third of the fresh water in Canada. As I said a moment ago, and as the minister himself noted, we have no assurance that it will always be this way and that our water resources will not, in time, create major troubles.
At various times, the alarm has been sounded by qualified authorities on the matter. For instance, I note in the newspaper La Voix de I'Est of November 2, 1966, that Mr. Peter White, president of the rural development of Brome county, sounded a warning that it may be proper to emphasize, and I quote:
-the Yamaska lake and river have become "a sewage lagoon".
Mr. Chairman, when it is realized that the Yamaska river supplies water to cities such as Granby and St. Hyacinthe, it is important


seriously to consider this warning by someone who is aware of the question. In the article mentioned here, the following is stated, and I quote:
Bacteriological contamination at St. Alphonse de Grandby, a small village nearby, is very serious. Animals have died through the years after drinking in the river. The river gives off a foul odour... the fish died some eight years ago.
The situation in that area is most alarming and it is imperative that we give it our whole attention.
On the other hand, Mr. R. L. Demers, engineer with the Quebec water control board, said, in an article published in La Presse on November 25, 1966:
It is later than we think as regards water pollution.
The premier of Quebec himself said, as reported in La Presse on February 14, 1967, and I quote:
If we do not use our water intelligently, if we misuse it, if we waste it unsparingly, and especially without any thought for the future, our water may not always constitute an inexhaustible resource.
As I am aware of the goodwill of the minister, aware also of his eagerness to help the population, I should like to have his co-operation, so that the threat to public health may eradicated from my area. I should also like to suggest that he use his influence with his colleagues, the Ministers of Forestry and Rural Development, of National Health and Welfare, and of Public Works (Messrs. Sauve, MacEachen, Mcllraith) so that a dike might be built on Yamaska River at Rapide Plat.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
In the summertime, Mr. Chairman, the Yamaska river reaches such a low level, below the dike known as "Penman", that it becomes a menace to public health. Fish die and the decay gives off a most unpleasant odour for the shore dwellers, and this smell I am sure, is also a menace to public health. I do think that it would cost very little to each of the departments concerned, to build a dike which would meet the general approval of the people of Saint-Hyacinthe and the other villages which also get their water supply from that river.
The minister will work, in a more or less distant future, in some part of my riding, where he will probably find the thorns to match the roses which I sent him earlier, from a political point of view, and I should like him to take advantage of that opportunity
June 20. 1967

to start working on his reputation so that, when the time comes to ask for votes in that part of my present riding, he will already be welcome.
I think the minister could very easily initiate a study into present conditions and their continuing disadvantages, as well as the menace to public health they constitute. I am sure that the minister would not want to have a summer cottage in the vicinity of a river which, during dry spells in the summer, gives off odours which are far from pleasant.
Therefore, I leave this problem with the minister. I am sure he will want to give favourable consideration to that question of pollution not only of water but also of air which is a menace, as I said before, to public health.
