Mr. Chairman, in just a few words I should like to express my disappointment at the news we heard this morning. I believe this is a very sad day for Canada and I think time will prove me right. The only thing that is perhaps not disappointing is that this will also prove to be a very sorry day for the Liberal party.
The fact that the decision announced this morning, as was pointed out by my colleague the hon. member for Timiskaming, was made purely and solely in the interests of the United States of America should also give the government and the Canadian people room for thought. In this respect we have experienced delay upon delay continuing for months and months. Suddenly, because the United States was given a real scare last week when overnight the Arab countries at least temporarily cut off their oil, the decision was made. I should like the Canadian people and the government to stop for one moment and consider whether this decision was really made in the interests of Canada.
The hon. member for Qu'Appelle said a few words on this subject and put forward certain suggestions. I wonder whether he has really stopped to think about what he said. He proposed, for example, that the gas should be sold on a cost for distance transported basis. If the line was to be built completely in Canada I would agree wholeheartedly with him. But in supporting the move to build the line through the United States he was in fact saying that United States customers should in perpetuity pay a cheaper rate than Canadian customers who live farther along the line. He 27053-m
Supply-Energy, Mines and Resources also reiterated-I believe the government shares his opinion-that this program will result in a much cheaper rate in eastern Canada. I am sorry that I do not share the optimism of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle any more than I share the optimism of the minister when he expresses the same view. Furthermore I defy either the minister or anyone else in the house to show one single instance where cost is a factor in our modern society. The cost factor does not enter into the picture at all. We all know or at least we should know that the only factor is what the traffic will bear, not what it costs to transport the gas.

The hon. member for Qu'Appelle, who is attempting to build up a reputation as a great nationalist, seems to defeat his purpose whenever he happens to deal with either gas or oil. I suggest that he review his ideas in this field. I was called to the telephone during one part of the hon. member's speech but I am told that he had some rather harsh words for the members of my party and the stand we have taken throughout the whole debate. I believe the hon. member paid a recent visit to northern Ontario and attended a meeting in my constituency. He must have seen with his own eyes how much support the views of his party receive in that part of the country. In fact, if he needs any further proof all he has to do is to look at the results of the recent election in Sudbury and he will find that the Conservative party got less than 10 per cent of the votes. The same is true in my riding.
There are one or two other points I should like to make. I have found that it is practically impossible for university students to find summer employment this year all across northern Ontario. The same is true for high school students in the top grades who are looking for jobs to pay for their further education. The big surge which followed the Texas Gulf crisis has now reached a plateau. Construction work is over. The Hollinger mine has announced that it is closing down and the Preston East Dome mine is to close before the end of the year. There is no work in prospect for our young people. Perhaps the minister will say that they can go to the United States and get jobs in the construction of the pipe line through the United States. Is this what the government is planning for our young people?
The government has made that part of the country a designated area, which may or may not stimulate development and build up industry there. However, I will tell the minister

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF ENERGY, MINES AND RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to take a few minutes to bring a couple of points to the attention of the minister, particularly in view of the political developments which have taken place in the world in the last few days. I think that the Israeli-Arab war should make it fairly clear to the minister that we must take a new look at the oil and gas industries in Canada. I point out to the committee that the Canadian oil industry is one of the largest industries in Canada. In fact, in the last 20 years it has developed from a $20 million a year industry to one worth over $1 billion in 1967. It is an industry which has greatly contributed to the balance of payments problem in Canada and to the welfare and prosperity of the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, and in fact British Columbia.
I do not want to go into the effects of the oil situation in Alberta so much as to try to relate to the minister the political implications of the recent world events and to quote to him a section from the Carter report which directly concerns the oil industry in Canada.
As the minister is quite well aware, oil has been discovered and is being produced in many parts of the world. New discoveries have been made in North Africa, Nigeria, the North Sea, the Middle East, Russia, and many other places. In most of these areas production is sometimes subject to political pressures. Combined with ever-increasing discoveries of oil there is an ever-increasing demand for oil in the world. There is an insatiable hunger for energy. For example, in 1966

33 million barrels per day were used, nearly double the amount used ten years previously. However, the point which must be kept in mind is that for every barrel of oil produced a new discovery must be made. In other words, use must be matched with new discoveries of oil and also account must be taken of the contemplated increase in the use of oil in the world.
In so far as Canada is concerned, and possibly the whole of North America, the security of our sources of supply of oil must be guaranteed. The importance of this has been emphasized by the political unrest in various parts of the world in recent years A few years ago the oil industry was nationalized in Iran as a result of which there was an interruption in the flow of oil to the western world for several weeks. This was followed by the Suez crisis in 1956. When Egypt took over the Suez Canal it cut off all the oil supplies that normally travelled through there. It also cut off the Arab pipe lines. As a result of the recent conflict between the Israelis and the Arabs oil supplies to Europe, North America, Japan, and in fact all parts of the western world, have been cut off.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
In considering the development of Canadian oil reserves, the security of our sources of supply must stand very high on our list of priorities. This was pointed out by the Borden royal commission. As a matter of fact, the Borden royal commission made this statement.
It is undoubtedly in the national interest that Canada should at least be in a position rapidly to make itself as independent as possible of imports which may be subject to interruption.
I do not pretend that there was an interruption in the supply of oil in Canada during the recent crisis but if the crisis had continued for a longer period of time it is quite possible that there would have been an interruption.
I would point out to the committee that Canada has relied increasingly on Middle East oil for use in the eastern Canadian market. In 1964 Venezuela, which up until recently has been our principal supplier of oil from overseas, supplied 71 per cent of the offshore supplies in eastern Canada and the Middle East supplied only 25 per cent. In 1965 Venezuela supplied 60 per cent and the Middle East 36 per cent. One can see that there is a decrease in the quantity of oil imported from Venezuela and an increase in the amount of oil imported from the Middle
June 20, 1967
COMMONS DEBATES	1735
East. The situation becomes even more pronounced in 1966 when Venezuela supplied only 50 per cent and the Middle East supplied 47 per cent. In two years the oil supply to eastern Canada from the Middle East has increased in volume from 25 per cent to 47 per cent.
It is worth noting that the considerable increase in oil imports which took place between 1965 and 1966 was of oil which originated in Nigeria and Libya. Almost the whole of the increase was represented by oil from Nigeria. The recent political disintegration of Nigeria is now common knowledge.
I bring these points to the attention of the minister principally because there is a section of the Carter report that could have a tremendous effect on oil exploration in Canada. I should like to refer the minister to page 326 of volume 4 of that report where it is said:
But if costs of conventional oil exploration continue to rise it is apparent that, if the tar sands are not now competitive with conventional crude, they will be competitive in the near future, and Canada's oil reserves, for all practical purposes, will be limitless. Devoting resources to the search for conventional oil is, or will become, unnecesary.
I should like the minister to look at that reference and give due consideration to it because the statement upon which the recommendations of the Carter report are predicated is an exaggeration. It does not take into consideration some of the political requirements of this country. For example, the statement falls short in at least three respects.
First of all, according to the statement the cost of conventional oil exploration continues to rise. As a matter of fact, just the opposite is the case. The cost of exploration for oil in western Canada is decreasing, and decreasing quite rapidly.
Second, it is stated that if the tar sands are not now competitive they soon will be. This is incorrect. The tar sands are not now competitive and it is difficult to see just at what time in the future they will be. It may be a very long period of time before tar sands developed oil will be able to compete with conventional oil.
Third, the statement totally disregards the fact that it takes at least five years to develop an oil project, particularly tar sands. It might also take the same length of time to develop a conventional flow of oil, build a pipe line and get the oil to the market. The statement made in the report of the Carter commission is quite premature. I do not think that the oil policy of this country should be predicated on such an assumption. I do not think that a 27053-1111
Supply-Energy, Mines and Resources change in taxation as it affects oil companies should be predicated on a statement of this sort.
I believe that the time has now come to take another look at the possibility of making this country self-sufficient in supplies of oil. As the minister is quite well aware, we are capable of producing more than enough oil for our own use. Yet the fact of the matter is that we still import large amounts of oil for use in eastern Canada. This is all well and good as long as political relationships in the world are harmonious. But I think an advanced country like Canada should be prepared to face all emergencies so far as the supply of energy is concerned, and the minister should look at the possibility of using Canadian oil only for all our needs.
I hope the minister will take seriously the comments I made about the Carter commission. It will probably be to the advantage of Canada to continue to develop oil reserves against the day when we do need far more oil on a daily basis than we require today.

subtopic: AETNA CASUALTY COMPANY OF CANADA

speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, June 6, 1967, consideration of the motion of Mr. Cameron (High Park) for the second reading of Bill No. C-112, to incorporate Aetna Casualty Company of Canada.

subtopic: AETNA CASUALTY COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on two previous occasions I have spoken on the motion for second reading of this bill. Anyone who tries to follow those remarks will have a rather difficult time because they are scattered throughout Hansard for various dates from May 30 of this year going back to last session. This is one of the bills that had their roots in the previous session, but were not passed. Frankly, I do not think it should be passed on this occasion either because, as I have said on a number of occasions about this and similar bills, it contains within it no provision whatever to permit the company to comply with the enunciated policy of the government of Canada or the feelings of nearly all members of parliament.
The gist of our objection to the incorporation of Aetna Casualty Company of Canada is that this company should within a reasonable period of time become Canadian owned, and it has not done so yet. During the last session we had similar discussions and felt that this point of view had been fairly well set out by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Gordon) and had been supported by other members of the house. It was felt that when and if this company again desired to become incorporated it would be forewarned of the attitude which might be taken, namely, that it should become a Canadian owned company within a reasonable period of time.
The intricacies of the company and its relationship to a United States company have been clearly set out by the sponsor of the bill. I might point out that even if we reach the stage of voting the sponsor would regretably not have the opportunity of making any concluding remarks about our objections because he appears to be somewhere else. In any event, he set out very clearly the relationship between this company and the parent company in Hartford, Connecticut.
The sponsor of the bill also referred to the company's premium structure, the number of policies it sold and its income, but nowhere in his remarks was there any intimation that the company or the sponsor of the bill, who is a Liberal, had given any recognition whatever to the declared policy of the government as announced very forcibly and clearly by the Prime Minister and as supported by a number of members of the cabinet.
When government policy on a matter such as this is delcared by the first minister of the cabinet, the Prime Minister, individuals and their supporters who come to parliament
June 20, 1967

seeking company incorporation under the umbrella and protection of the parliament of Canada have a duty to see that their bill complies with the announced policy. This bill fails to do that and I submit that the individual who-

subtopic: AETNA CASUALTY COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that many members of the house will recall that I view nearly all private incorporations of insurance companies with a jaundiced eye. I have a particularly jaundiced eye in respect of this company. I have been reading the statement the sponsor made on May 30, as recorded in Hansard at page 752, about the astonishing generality of this company. It is to be a subsidiary of the Aetna Casualty and Surety Company of Hartford, Connecticut. That company is a corporation carrying on a substantial general insurance business in the United States with its subsidiary, the Standard Fire Insurance Company, and writes business on all classes of insurance.
The sponsor told us that the Aetna Casualty and Surety Company was organized in 1907 and operated as a partially owned subsidiary of Aetna Life Insurance Company until late in 1964 when a reorganization was conducted under which all the shares were transferred to and are now being held by a trustee for the shareholders of the Aetna Life Insurance Company.
The Aetna Life Insurance Company has had a similarly chequered career. It was incorporated and commenced business in 1853. The Aetna Life and Casualty organization now carries on business throughout the United States of America. The sponsor then tells us that the Aetna Life Insurance Company commenced business in Canada over 100 years ago. Apparently in 1960 the Aetna Life Insurance Company made an offer to the shareholders of the Excelsior Life Insurance Company of Toronto to purchase approximately 70 per cent of its outstanding shares. I suppose this is the way this company finally came into Canada.
There has been absolutely no concealment whatever that this is a foreign-owned corporation. It is owned entirely in the United States, and there is no suggestion that there are any other shareholders than those residing in the United States. At one point the sponsor of the bill had this to say:
All but four of the present employees are Canadians-
Private Bills
He was referring to the Aetna Casualty and Surety Company of Hartford which has claim offices in Toronto, Montreal, Quebec city, Hamilton, Winnipeg, Calgary and Vancouver. It would be interesting to know just who those four employees are, because I suspect that they are not office boys or stenographers. I suspect that one might find these four employees sitting in the executive offices of this company in Canada. The rest of the employees, who may be Canadian citizens, are not holding the important positions that these four unidentified, non-Canadians are holding.
[DOT] (6:10 p.m.)
There is another point I would have liked the sponsor to develop a little further. The hon. member for High Park (Mr. Cameron) said:
A financing plan has been developed to provide the capital and surplus necessary without impairing the balance of trade position of either Canada or the United States.
I presume he means the balance of payments position, because this is a purely financial matter. I should like to know what this plan is. Does it mean that this company is not merely to collect the savings of Canadians through insurance policies but is to collect the savings of Canadians by means of loans, presumably, and debentures in order to finance its operations in this country? I imagine this is what it will do, because it is the time-honoured method by which foreign companies have been able to extend their holdings in Canadian development, Canadian industry, Canadian resources and, as we see in this bill, Canadian financial institutions. I should like to know just what this particular financing plan, about which the sponsor was rather coy, might be. The sponsor made another rather interesting statement:
The establishment of this Canadian company will create for Canada additional employment, additional capital funds and, as previously mentioned, additional capacity for the insurance market.
Let us deal with those three great advantages in allowing this foreign-owned company to move into the Canadian economy. It is said it will create additional employment in Canada. Well, perhaps it will. But I suggest that every policy written by the Aetna Casualty Company after this bill is passed will be written at the expense of an existing insurance company. There is, after all, a very definite limit to the amount of funds that are available for investing in the policies of this type of company. Therefore I doubt that there will really be any additional employment as a

June 20. 1967
Private Bills
result of the incorporation of this company, or if there is it will be additional employment which will increase the rates because it will increase the costs of insurance companies doing business in Canada.
The sponsor says that the establishment of this company will provide additional capital funds. I wonder how that statement can be squared with the statement about the financing plan that will provide capital without affecting the balance of payments position between Canada and the United States. Obviously, if this company is to provide additional capital it must come from somewhere outside the country, and if it comes from somewhere outside the country it is bound to have some effect on our balance of payments position.
The final praise for this company, the final argument in favour of our accepting it, is that it will provide additional capacity for the insurance market. I have yet to hear any insurance company complaining that it has not the capacity to service everybody who tries to buy a policy from it. In fact, I am sure we all know that the major expenditure of insurance companies is the commissions and wages of agents who go out and try to sell policies. I do not think any additional capacity is required in the insurance market in that regard. I am quite sure the present insurance companies can write all the policies that the people of Canada want to have written. I believe that the present insurance companies can carry all the load of insurance that Canadian business wishes to have carried. It seems to me a rather preposterous idea to suggest that this company will provide additional capacity for the insurance market. What it will do is bring about additional costs to the whole insurance industry of this country, as does every new insurance company incorporated by this parliament.
I would report for the benefit of hon. members of the house the words of the inspector of insurance when I asked him in committee whether in his opinion the incorporation of new insurance companies was calculated to create the sort of competition that would reduce costs for the insurance policyholder. I will always remember that the inspector of insurance, after carefully considering my question, said: Well, I admit that in my department they are beginning to wonder whether it is necessary to have all these new insurance company incorporations. This was, of course, as close as one could in fairness expect a civil servant to come to criticizing the policies adopted by the government and
[Mr. Cameron (Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands) .1
the parliament of Canada. Obviously he had very grave doubts as to the benefits to be derived from incorporating more insurance companies.
I should like to stress again the way in which this bill completely flouts the announced policy of the government of Canada and of the parliament of Canada with regard to the foreign ownership of financial institutions. I am quite sure that the committee of which I am a member, and this parliament, did not take the action it took with regard to the Mercantile Bank of Canada as an isolated instance. It was a case in point which underlined the danger, in the view of the government and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp), of allowing non-Canadian interests to get a grip on Canadian financial institutions. This is one of those institutions that to my mind should be firmly in Canadian hands.
Let us look at it this way, Mr. Speaker. These people are not in business for amusement or for entertainment. They are in business to make money. They are going to make money, and we have not yet been told who is to provide the capital and the surplus with which they are to make money. We have had a rather contradictory statement from the sponsor of the bill. But they are in business to make money. They are going to make money out of the Canadian economy. They are going to persuade Canadian people, Canadian businesses and Canadian groups of all sorts to gamble with them on casualty insurance.
It may be true, as the sponsor of the bill says, that it is the intention of the Aetna Casualty and Surety Company, the parent company, to leave any underwriting profits in the Canadian company to strengthen its financial structure. This sounds like a very noble and righteous attitude on the part of the company. It will be what I think the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Winters) is fond of calling "a good corporate citizen"; it will keep its money in Canada.
I would point out, Mr. Speaker, that every large Canadian subsidiary of an American company has expanded its operations in precisely this way, through what are rather euphemistically called internally generated savings or retained earnings. In blunter parlance, of course, this means excess or surplus profits. This company will leave them here, of course, because it intends to expand its operations. It will expand its operations at the expense of the existing companies in this country.
While I hold no particular brief for any insurance company, domestic or foreign, if I
June 20, 1967

had to make a choice I would rather see my fellow Canadian citizens have the opportunity to make money out of the rest of us than have people from another country do so. I would be very strenuously opposed to the passage of the bill at this time, particularly when the government has taken a firm position with regard to another financial institution, a position which may well be challenged in a few years time, as I warned the Minister of Finance only a few days ago. When it is challenged I can hear Mr. Rockefeller saying to the government of Canada and the Minister of Finance that they allowed the Aetna Casualty Company of Hartford to come into Canada and set up a company wholly owned by American capital and asking why we are discriminating against him. This is what he said when he came here last time. We will give him an added argument to support his contention that the Canadian parliament was guilty of gross discrimination against the Mercantile Bank of Canada.
[DOT] (6:20 p.m.)
I feel very strongly on this matter because of my attitude toward the whole insurance industry, both domestic and foreign. I think that before long we will have to move very quickly in this field because it will become part of any program in the direction of investment, if we are going to develop Canada in the way we want to develop it. If we allow companies which have the privilege of collecting the savings of Canadians to be in foreign hands, our task will be rendered more difficult. So I am very strenuously opposed to the passage of this bill and I hope the house will reject it.

subtopic: AETNA CASUALTY COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very interested in the comments that have been made on this bill both by the sponsor and by some of my colleagues. I hope the day will come when such statements do not have to be made, when a statement such as the one I made earlier regarding the national ownership of our resources will be taken for granted. I hope no one will consider allowing the ingress of United States businessmen into a field which affects the lives and aspirations of Canadians any more than they will allow a situation to develop similar to what took place today when the government showed no offence at the fact that an American board made a ruling which gave them an opportunity to get off the hook.
The Aetna Casualty Company is probably no worse or no better than any of the other
Private Bills
insurance companies operating in this field. It is true of this company, as it is of car insurance and crop damage insurance companies whose agents receive a percentage of the premiums that are paid by individuals, that the administration costs exceed the normal costs of good operation. As we learned last year, Aetna Casualty Company has been doing business in Canada for a number of years in several fields. One of their subsidiaries is the Excelsior Life Insurance Company which is owned entirely by them and has been allowed to grow in Canada until it has become one of the largest life insurance companies. They have also been operating a branch office in Canada under the agency of Dale and Company of Montreal. It is interesting to note that part of Expo was insured by this company. Perhaps at the time of the incorporation of the company I should have asked the sponsor what aspect of Expo was insured by them, whether they issued insurance against inability to meet the deadline for the opening of Expo or whether it was insurance against fire losses.
It is a fact that for a number of years now this company has operated in Canada in both the life insurance and casualty fields. It is also true that for many years the Aetna Casualty Company has been operating from Hartford and has been under the control of the Department of Industry to the extent that it is covered by the foreign Insurance Companies Act.
I had the opportunity of talking to some of the officials of the company whom I found to be very astute businessmen. In my opinion they are not unlike the type of people we would want to run a Canadian company. They were of the opinion that it was going to be very difficult for them to meet the commitment which I think most people in Canada would like to see met by companies coming into Canada to do business. I think there are two types of companies. There are those that come here with risk capital, are willing to put up their money to do business in our country and are prepared to offer a large employment potential. Second, there are the companies which offer very limited employment but which accumulate large sums of money in a very short period of time. This money is advanced to the subsidiaries by the headquarters located outside of Canada at very small risk, and it is only necessary for them to have this money available.
We find in the bill that the incorporation of the company is asked for by a number of

June 20, 1967
Private Bills
lawyers. It seems to me that the fact that a lawyer who is resident in Canada is being asked to represent a new company proves that they are not really establishing a company but are setting up a holding operation for some other group. With the exception of Melvin Kirkland Kenny, an insurance executive, and Albert Bruce Matthews who is listed as an executive, I would presume the others are only acting in trust and are in fact what are called, in fairly vulgar vernacular, "fronts" for other persons. If we are really going to carry out what has been said to be the intention of the Prime Minister and certainly of the former minister of finance, that is, put this type of operation under Canadian control to provide funds for investment in Canada, then we should seriously consider this matter.
Clause 6 of the bill lists the fields in which this company wishes to operate. It is obvious that the money which is put up in the various fields will never be collected. This may even be true of automobile insurance where the rate of payment is much higher than in other fields.
Many of us wonder how long it will take the Liberal party, or whatever party may form the government of Canada, to make up their mind to enter the field of insurance and provide what is obviously a necessary protection for Canadians through the establishment of a crown corporation so that the money invested in such companies can be used for other purposes. This field has been partly covered by the Canada Pension Plan. I believe we are developing a pension plan that meets many of the requirements which were not previously met by insurance companies. One of these was the need for sums secured by life insurance policies to bear some relationship to the need of the person insured. It is a fact that during the depression people found it difficult to keep up payments of premiums on policies, and in many cases were forced to abandon their policies. After saving and scrimping for many years to meet the premiums of an endowment policy for $10,000 or $20,000 which during the depression years was probably equivalent to $100,000 today, they lost everything.
[DOT] (6:30 p.m.)
We have attempted to remove some of the abuse from the insurance field, particularly with endowment policies and pensions, and have appointed a government agency to administer the Canada Pension Plan. We have not done the same thing to cover such risks as hail, for example, or some of the other risks 
that other companies are covering, such as forgery, falling aircraft, explosions, earthquakes, automobile accidents, water damage, wind storms, and so on. These are risks which-involve, in my opinion, a large premium. It is almost like allowing a company to print money.
That alone would be bad enough, Mr. Speaker, but we even let these companies come into Canada and speculate against the interests of our own people, who provide the money for this speculation in the form of premiums. The corporation concerned at the same time accumulates a large profit.
It is all very well for the hon. member who is sponsoring the bill to say that this money will not be taken out of the country. Certainly, I am sure the superintendent of insurance will see to it that enough money is kept in Canada to meet the commitments that these companies make. Nevertheless, in view of the undistributed profits and the reserves that these companies accumulate, in my opinion the government should control this field in the interests of the general public.
It is interesting to note that if you want, for example, to build a house in my area Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation will not lend money if the house is to be serviced with a septic tank. They do not say that a septic tank is undesirable, but they do say that too many septic tanks close together are undesirable, which is probably true. However, this corporation was not set up to decide on a national housing policy for Canada. The officials of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation suggest that these people borrow money from insurance companies or trust companies if the house they want to build is to have a septic tank.
These corporation officials tell these people: "We are a crown agency set up to help you build a house. We will not let you build it where you want because, in our own small way, we want to restrict you or put a roadblock in the way of your building your house in this area". As a result, the insurance company enters the field and uses for mortgage purposes the money deposited with that company. The policy holders do not get any return from that investment unless, of course, they collect on their insurance.
Suppose I were to protect myself against forgery, Mr. Speaker. If someone gave me a bad cheque I doubt whether the amount would nearly equal the premiums I had paid to the company, particularly if I were a small businessman. Yet these companies are allowed to come into Canada and issue policies
June 20. 19S7

Private Bills
of insurance, collect these vast sums by way of premiums, and then plough this money back in the form of mortgages and other instruments.
I attended a committee for most of the afternoon which was sitting in camera and doing a very good job. I found almost total unanimity about most of the work the committee was doing. I can remember that during the last five years I have stood in my place during this same hour and was criticized, browbeaten, told that I was stupid, was a communist, was a fascist, and so on, yet the same people who accused me of these things were sitting on that committee agreeing to matters which we legitimately tried to persuade them to accept four or five years ago. At that time we had absolutely no support.
I should like to see some of the members who sponsor these bills have the gumption to tell these companies that we in Canada are not interested in having all these insurance companies. We do not need a proliferation of 10,000 insurance companies. We are not going to solve the unemployment problem by having policy holders all over the country starving to death. If only these members would do this these companies which abuse the needs of the Canadian public would not receive incorporation from this parliament.
Aetna is proposing to cover risks which are already covered. I am not saying they are being dishonest or that the sponsor of the bill is being dishonest. I give both of them the benefit of the doubt by saying that they do not know any better. But the sponsors of these bills are not telling the Canadian people what these companies are doing. This bill concerns the Aetna Insurance Company of Hartford, Connecticut, which wants to set up a company in this country with a board of directors composed of four or five Canadians in order to comply with the terms which have been laid down for the incorporation of such companies. The bill says that the capitalization of this company shall be $5 million, divided into shares of $50.
Aetna Insurance Company of Hartford, Connecticut, could set up a thousand insurance companies tomorrow on the strength of the companies they already own. They are not selling $5 million worth of stock divided in $50 shares. This stock will never be sold; it will probably never appear on the market. It does not need to be sold because the company itself could put up that sum tomorrow.
[DOT] (6:40 p.m.)
They have already done so. They came here some years ago and established the Excelsior
Life Insurance Company. It grew into a very large and responsible company and it had no difficulty about raising money at any time. Surely hon. members should give some consideration to what is done with these large sums which these insurance companies accumulate. Suppose our old age pensioners were receiving $25 more than they needed, and put this amount of money away under their mattresses. I believe we should soon find ourselves in serious trouble. I heard the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) say that the cost of raising old age pensions would amount to $800 million-a terrible sum. Well, we covered about three quarters of the amount proposed, and the cost amounted to about $200 million. As I pointed out, most of this goes back to the government in a very short time after three or four transactions. Suppose this extra money were placed in the hands of an insurance company. It would be the same as putting it into savings. It is true protection is provided, but much of the money has to be held. This money is reinvested by the companies. Possibly some hon. members may be thinking that they will be defeated eventually in an election and it would be nice for them to be considered in this group.
The point I am making is that we are not interested in merely having Canadians on the board of directors. We, in this group, would like to have Canadians on the board because we believe that eventually the Canadian business community must have the overriding interest in things Canadian. When an insurance company such as this makes an application for a charter to collect money, that money should be used for the benefit of some Canadian enterprise, be it in the mortgage field or insurance protection field.
Obviously the money that is collected does not all go into protection. Any insurance company that collected $1 million and paid out $1 million in claims would not be coming to Canada or anywhere else. If it is a business

operation it collects $1 million, pays out much less than that in claims, and invests the rest.
The President of the Privy Council (Mr. Gordon), and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Winters), the first in his book on economic prospects and Canadian development, and the second in speeches in this house, have said that companies must be good Canadian corporate citizens. I think the Canadians being appointed to many of these boards are not necessarily good corporate citizens. They are citizens who are being employed for a specific purpose.
The day must come soon when we strengthen our Department of Insurance and make it responsbile for recommending what insurance companies should be added to the present total. The Aetna Casualty Company will not do one thing in Canada that cannot be done by some company already established. If it were to offer one kind of insurance that nobody else offers, it would serve a need and would deserve consideration. The wording of the amendment is:
-to provide alternative employment for employees of the corporation who may be laid off as a result thereof.
This is the wording which is suggested should be added to clause 17 (4) (b).
If the mine in the constituency which I represent, which is one of the Dosco mines, had been included by the minister in this legislation, if the wording as suggested by the amendment of the hon. member for York South should be adopted, the employees of that mine of course would be ensured of the protection which would be provided by the amended clause.
As has been pointed out earlier in the debate-and this bears repetition-a telegram dated today was directed to the Prime Minister and undoubtedly also to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources as well as to members from the area, from the president and other officers of the United Mine Workers of America, District 26. I think this should be put on the record. It was referred to earlier during the question period. I will read it quickly:
United Mine Workers of America District 26 shocked and dismayed over federal Bill C-135 to exclude McBean mine in the proposed crown corporation.
What follows refers to something I mentioned during the resolution stage:
This action completely contradicts Prime Minister's statement December 29, 1966-
The quotation is taken from the minister's statement.
-when he said and I quote:
Assured of the participation of the government of Nova Scotia, the government of Canada is prepared to ask parliament to establish a suitable crown corporation-the composition and powers of which will be defined by the two governments at an early date-to acquire, reorganize and manage the coal mining interest of the Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation.
That is the end of that part of the quotation. The telegram continues:
[The Chairman.]
This automatically includes Acadia, which is a subsidiary of Dosco.
Then there is another quotation from the Prime Minister's statement:
The government of Canada and the government of Nova Scotia believe that a rigid adherence to a fixed timetable to reduce the level of coal production might involve unnecessary hardship on the dependent communities. Consequently the rationalization of the mines will be related to the success in the introduction of new industries.
That is the end of that quotation.
So that McBean or any other colliery would have to be kept in operation until new industries were introduced to provide alternate employment as promised by Prime Minister Pearson. Further on in the Prime Minister's statement he indicated that the government of the province of Nova Scotia would be held responsible for the smaller independent operations and the federal government would be responsible for the Dosco mines which automatically again includes McBean.
Then the telegram concludes in this way:
The officers of District 26 United Mine Workers of America urgently request a meeting of representatives of the federal government, provincial government and the United Mine Workers of America District 26 to clarify this misunderstanding.
May I repeat that if this mine had been taken in along with the other Dosco mines as was promised, this clause, of course, would apply and, if the amendment of the hon. member for York South is passed-I hope it will be and I commend it to all members-the workers at this mine would be guaranteed alternative employment.
When I asked the minister a question about this mine he said at one point that it would cost approximately $2 million to continue it to the end of 1967. At another point he said that perhaps this money should be used to continue the mine and at another point he said that perhaps it should be used for another purpose.
We do not know whether he will be the minister, but he has also stated that perhaps it will take close to three months or five months to get the corporation working. As I said before, the Donald report suggested that there should be resources from this mine until 1970. We are not clear what the minister has said, but if this mine were taken in under the terms of clause 17, as was promised by the Prime Minister on December 29 of last year, then these miners, the men working on the surface and, the office staff would be protected.

A few days ago we read in the press that the Presbyterian Church in Canada had taken steps to increase the pensions of its ministers already retired. Some of the automobile companies do this. Many of these things have been won, let it be said, by collective bargaining. But nevertheless the principle that people who are already retired have a right to compensation for the increase in the cost of living, and a right to share in the increased standard of living, has been established in this country. The government itself has recognized this principle in at least two pieces of legislation. The Canada Pension Plan has in it a provision under which from the year 1968 on increases to compensate for the increased cost of living are automatic. On June 12, 1967, Mr. Speaker, as recorded in Hansard on page 1397, I put the following question to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Greene):
Since March 22, 1967. has his department negotiated with the agriculture department of Quebec on assistance to potato producers? If so, what are the results?

June 20, 1967

feels this is an urgent question of national importance, he could bring it up on the adjournment motion.
I raised this question, Mr. Speaker, because it is very important for thousands of potato producers in Quebec as well as in the other provinces.
I believe the 1966 potato crop in Canada was the best in 40 years. As of March 1, 1967, our warehouse stock showed a 43 per cent increase over that of the preceding year, in spite of a high volume of sales to foreign countries.
On March 22, 1967, the federal Minister of Agriculture announced the adoption of a program authorizing the Agricultural Stabilization Board to provide a support price of $1.65 per barrel of Canada No. 1 potatoes sent to starch plants.
In areas where there are no starch plants -as in the province of Quebec-and where there may be an important surplus of potatoes, the associations and groups of producers wishing to participate in the federal support program were to submit the terms of their propositions to the Agricultural Stabilization Board.
I am told that potato growers and other groups interested in that farm produce made certain proposals to the Agricultural Stabilization Board.
The hon. member for Riviere-du-Loup-Temiscouata (Mr. Gendron) and I accompanied such a group in April when they met representatives of the Department of Agriculture to discuss the problem.
Another program was offered the Quebec potato growers, whereby surpluses would be used in feed rations intended for cattle. This alternative did not seem to please the growers, most of whom did not own boilers or Choppers and, moreover, were afraid to destroy their feed system based on balanced rations.

So, the crop of 1966 has brought about some problems and it has been necessary for the government to institute a program to bring about some relief.
The level of assistance available under the Agricultural Stabilization Board is 75 cents per hundredweight and in addition the feed value of the potatoes, which is estimated at at least 25 cents per hundredweight, would accrue to the producer. This program is in effect in five other provinces and to date in excess of one million hundredweight of pota-toese have been committed under this program.
It may be true that there may be areas in which the livestock feeding program is not of immediate assistance. I understand from the minister and from his officials that consideration is still being given to alleviating this particular hardship. I know that if any relief is available in this regard, the announcement will be made by the minister at a later date.

IMMIGRATION-DENIAL OF LANDED IMMIGRANT STATUS TO GREEK SHEPHERD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 13 I directed a question to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration. I said:
I have his letter denying landed immigrant status to a Greek shepherd, and I should like to ask the minister *whether Moses, who looked after sheep for 40 years, or King David, who was also a shepherd, would have been admitted to Canada under the present regulations.
I did not receive any answer to this query of June 13 and I should like to elucidate further on the matter. This question was discussed at some length during the adjournment debate on June 12. At that time some remarks were made about this man, Mr. Sistanis, who is under order for deportation after having appeared before a special inquiry officer of the immigration branch and the appeal board.
June 20, 1967
1766	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
I based my remarks which I made on June 12 entirely on the fact that on April 21 there had been a revolution in Greece and this young man, who came to Canada in 1966, did not wish to return to that dictatorship country. I have in my hand clippings from the Ottawa Journal, the Ottawa Citizen, the Toronto Star and other papers referring to the fact that since April 21 Greece has been under a martial dictatorship. An editorial in the Toronto Star of May 12 referred to a statement that Canada was going to devote $1.5 million as aid to Greece. This was severely criticized. A paragraph in the editorial reads:
The sum of $1,500,000 is not much by modern budgetary standards. But we can think of better uses for it than pouring it down a dictator's gun barrels.
I should like to point out that this man, Mr. Sistanis, is still in the country although he has purchased a ticket back to Greece. He is waiting for a seat on an airplane because he has been told he must get out.
I want to emphasize that we are forcing upon a Greek citizen something that we did not enforce in respect of the Polish art treasures which came into Canada in 1940. This morning I spent some time looking up the historical facts in connection with these Polish art treasures. They were sent from Poland to France by way of the Black Sea and Rumania before the advance of the Germans in 1939. When it looked as though France was going to fall in 1940, these Polish art treasures worth millions and millions of dollars were sent from the south end of France to Canada and were stored for a short time at the central experimental farm in Ottawa. Following the breakdown of the established Polish government in 1940 these Polish art treasures were moved to other places in Canada, and I do not believe for a moment that their destination was unknown as intimated at the time.
When I read references in Maclean's magazine, the Canadian Forum and Hansard for 1945, 1946, 1947, 1953 and 1958 I did not And a pretty picture of Canadian diplomacy. We held on to these Polish art treasures in Canada and kept telling the Polish people who were asking for the return of their prized possessions that we could not send these back to them because the government that sent them to us was no longer in power.


We continually told them that it was impossible for us to return them to the new government of Poland because the government from which we received them was no longer in existence. We kept this up for a period of years.
One of the documents I have in my hand here is a letter dated February 13, 1948, from the under secretary of state for external affairs, one L. B. Pearson, to a Dr. Bielski who was charge d'affaires at the Polish legation in Ottawa. In part it reads:
As we agreed with your solicitors, we are communicating the information to you for any further action you and your solicitors may wish to take.
That was dated February 13, 1948, and the established Polish government of 1945 had been asking over and over again where the treasures were. For three years we held them back. If we were willing to send these Polish treasures to various areas in Quebec and keep them away from the new Polish government I do not see why we should have to inform a genuine, genial Greek that he has to get back to Greece and get back there as quickly as possible, despite the fact Greece has a new government, a military dictatorship.
A week from Thursday we are going to be welcoming a Greek to this country, and as far as I know he has not even got a work permit. When he is here he will be opening hospitals and laying cornerstones, and we in the house here will have to shake him by the hand and tell him how wonderful we think the Greeks are. If we are to greet him with open arms here at parliament hill I can not understand why we should order this Greek shepherd to be deported.
This is supposed to be a classless country. Are we going to kick this Greek shepherd out of this country and welcome a Greek prince and welcome the Greek King and Queen on September 4? I say to you that this country should have a reputation for political asylum. This young lad of 23 does not want to return to Greece under its new government and does not want to be forced to go back.
Only since supper time tonight, June 20, did I receive a printed form from Ministre de la Main-d'Oeuvre et de l'lmmigration, which I suppose means Manpower and Immigration. It is stated that there are new selection policies for immigration. At page 5 it is stated that this is a summary of the new selection policy for immigrants, and there is a suggestion that no longer will a man have to have
June 20, 1967	COMMONS
seven years education as set out on page 21 of th.e white paper on immigration, but that he may have slightly less education if he has a job to go to, if he has relatives in this country and if he is under 35 years of age. Nicholas Sistanis has all these qualifications. He has six years education and in April the minister said that apprenticeship time will count; that three years apprenticeship will be taken into consideration. This man was five years a shepherd and three years a housepainter in Greece.
This young man qualifies under the apprenticeship clause, so far as the statement is concerned, under two headings, agriculture and housepainting and because of his youth and his ability I suggest he should not be forced to go back to Greece. We are welcoming a Greek prince here next week and the Greek King and Queen on September 4, and I say we should welcome a common ordinary Greek who wants to stay here with his uncle and aunt and his cousins in the town of Weston in the riding of York-Humber. He is qualified in every way under the new immigration selection policy as set out in the statement received by members of parliament this evening. If they opened their mail boxes at supper time they will have this statement. If they have not, they will get it tomorrow.
[DOT] (10:20 p.m.)
I simply ask that the Department of Manpower and Immigration allow this man to remain in Canada. I sincerely ask that he be given the same kind of treatment that was given to the Polish art treasures. That is, that no speedy action be taken in respect of this young lad who should be allowed to stay. He is here now. He has not worked since he came here. I sincerely ask that he be given the same kind of treatment as the Polish art treasures; that is, that no speedy action be taken on him at all and he be allowed to settle in like the Polish art treasures which were in this country from 1940 to 1949 or 1950 before any action was taken to send them back to Poland.
Let us treat a genuine, genial, Greek, who is a human being, as well as we treated those painted Polish pictures. At least they stayed in Canada for years before we returned them to their home country. We should treat this Greek better by allowing him to stay in this country, where he wishes to settle, where his aunt, uncle and cousins reside, and where he 27053-113J

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is not much to add to what we said when this question was raised on the late show about two weeks ago. The minister then informed the hon. member, through myself, that this man about whom the hon. member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan) speaks did not comply with the immigration conditions and was asked to leave Canada. He was here as a visitor; he did not comply with the conditions and he was asked to go back at the end of his stay.
There is another factor to consider when we talk about fairness. Perhaps the hon. member for York-Humber would like to consider this. If all visitors, or a good proportion of them, who come to this country were allowed to remain, it would certainly be most unfair to all their compatriots in their country of origin who had gone through the procedures necessary, who had been to the immigration offices abroad, made application to remain here permanently, had their X-rays and all their medical checks and so on, if we just let them wait endlessly while we treated in a favoured way those who came here as visitors.
